cards.hook: Put skew is a hedging tax, not a crash forecast.
cards.body: Index put skew - the premium of downside implied vol over upside - is far steeper than the actual asymmetry of returns justifies. The driver isn't a better crash forecast. It's **structural demand for downside insurance**: pensions, funds with drawdown mandates, and overwriters all lean the same way, bidding puts and pressing calls. That persistent imbalance is a risk premium, harvestable through risk reversals or put ratios. The catch is what you inherit. Selling skew leaves you short the exact tail everyone else is paying to avoid, so the premium is rent for standing under the thing that falls.
cards.depth: Equity index skew steepened structurally after 1987, when the crash taught dealers that downside gaps are real and put demand became permanent. Pre-1987 index options showed little skew at all. The premium you collect selling it is compensation for absorbing that lesson on everyone else's behalf.

cards.hook: Denmark wants to give you copyright in your own face.
cards.body: In mid-2025 Denmark's government proposed something no copyright regime has done: granting each citizen an intellectual-property right in their own **face, body, and voice**. The theory reframes deepfakes as infringement rather than defamation or privacy harm, so a person could demand takedown of a synthetic likeness the way a studio pulls a pirated film. It reportedly covers realistic digital imitations and carves out parody and satire. The mechanism matters because IP rights transfer, license, and survive. A privacy claim dies with you, but a copyright-style likeness right could be assigned, inherited, and enforced platform-side.
cards.depth: Contrast the US patchwork: right of publicity is state law, varies wildly, and in most states is a commercial-appropriation tort, not property a platform must proactively honor. A copyright-style frame flips the default from opt-out enforcement to opt-in licensing, and hands the takedown machinery of copyright to individuals.

cards.hook: The hot hand was real. The famous study had a bug.
cards.body: For thirty years the hot hand in basketball was the textbook case of humans seeing patterns in randomness. Then in 2018 Miller and Sanjurjo found a subtle flaw in the original analysis. If you take a finite sequence of coin flips and measure how often a head follows a head, the answer is **below 50 percent, not equal to it** - a selection effect baked into how streaks get counted. Correcting for it, the original data actually showed a real hot-hand effect. The lesson isn't about basketball. It's that a bias correction you never thought to check can flip a conclusion outright.
cards.depth: The bias: conditioning on 'the previous flip was heads' shortens the pool of eligible next-flips in a way that favors tails. In a length-100 sequence the expected conditional rate runs a few points under half. Small sample, invisible skew, thirty years of confident citation.

cards.hook: A reward next month barely exists to your brain today.
cards.body: Delay discounting is the rate at which a future reward loses value as it moves further away. Everyone discounts; the ADHD curve just drops **steeper and faster**, so a payoff two weeks out carries almost no motivational pull in the present. This is why 'it matters for my career' fails to start a task while 'it's due in an hour' works instantly - the deadline drags the reward into the now. The move isn't more willpower. It's engineering the payoff closer: stake money you lose today, tell someone you'll report back tonight, or split the goal so a real win lands within the hour.
cards.depth: Same mechanism sits under why body-doubling and deadlines work. They don't add discipline, they compress the distance to a consequence. Anything that converts a distant abstract reward into a near concrete one is working the curve instead of fighting it.

cards.hook: Why isn't fifteen years of daily returns fifteen years of evidence?
cards.body: You've got thousands of daily observations and a clean equity curve. Statistics only pay you for one thing, though, and it isn't row count. Give it a beat before you read on. The answer: **independence**. Daily returns clump into regimes - one bull, one crash, one recovery - so a model fit across 2010 to 2021 mostly saw a single macro environment wearing thousands of costumes. Its effective sample might be two or three. That's why strategies 'validated on fifteen years' die in year sixteen: they were tuned against a handful of regimes and read the calendar as the sample.
cards.depth: Same trap hides in cross-validation on time series: shuffle the days and adjacent-regime leakage inflates every score. The honest count is regimes survived, not observations logged - which is why walk-forward across distinct environments tells you more than another decade inside the same one.

cards.hook: Your covered call is a short put in disguise.
cards.body: Put-call parity forces it. Long stock plus a short call equals a short put plus a bond, so a **covered call and a cash-secured put** at the same strike and expiry carry the same payoff shape, the same max profit, and the same downside. The 'conservative income' label on covered calls and the 'risky' label on naked puts describe one identical risk. If you would not sell the put, you have no business writing the call. The only real differences are financing, dividends, and early-assignment path, not the exposure you are actually taking on.
cards.depth: Parity says C minus P equals S minus the discounted strike. Rearranged, long-stock-short-call equals a short put plus lending the strike. The bond piece is a constant vertical shift, so it moves the breakeven but not the shape. Assignment timing and dividend capture differ, which is why the two are not literally interchangeable in a taxable, dividend-paying account.

cards.hook: The MFN you grant is a free option on your future deals.
cards.body: A most-favored-nations clause promises party A your best terms. Its real cost is not felt today. It is that every future negotiation now carries a hidden liability: any concession you make to party B ratchets back to A automatically. You have **written a free option** on your own future flexibility, and the counterparty holds it at zero premium. Seasoned drafters price this by narrowing scope hard: same category of licensee, same territory, same term length, economic terms only. The unscoped MFN across all future deals is the one that quietly detonates years later.
cards.depth: Scope levers that actually contain it: comparability baskets, so only genuinely like deals trigger the clause; economic-only, excluding creative or approval rights; a sunset date; and a carve-out for affiliate or bundled transactions. The broadest version, all terms and all future deals, silently turns every later negotiation into a three-party negotiation you never invited the first party to attend.

cards.hook: In 2006, one fund lost $6.6 billion on a gas spread.
cards.body: Amaranth Advisors bet on natural gas calendar spreads through trader Brian Hunter. The thesis itself was not crazy. The problem was scale: the fund's positions were a reported outsized fraction of open interest in the contracts it traded, so Amaranth was no longer betting on the market, it had **become the market**. When the spread turned against it in September 2006, there was no one to sell to at a sane price, and every attempt to exit pushed the spread further away. Roughly $6.6 billion evaporated in about a week. The lesson is not that spreads are dangerous. It is that size relative to liquidity is its own greek.
cards.depth: Liquidity risk is invisible in a backtest that assumes you trade at the mid. It surfaces only when your own exit is the largest order in the book. The tell is simple: if unwinding your position would move the price against you, you do not really hold a position of that size, you hold a claim you cannot actually sell. Size to the exit, not the entry.

cards.hook: Toddlers barely learn from a screen a live person would teach them.
cards.body: Show a toddler under about two and a half a task on video, and show another child the identical task performed live, and the live group learns it markedly better. Researchers call the gap the **video deficit**. Same content, same demonstrator, but the screen version underperforms until roughly age three. The likely mechanism is that very young brains treat flat, non-responsive video as not-quite-real, and learning at that age is tuned to live social interaction. The practical read: 'educational' video for a one-year-old is mostly entertainment, whatever the box promises.
cards.depth: The rescue is contingency, not resolution. In studies, real-time video chat where the adult responds live produces close to in-person learning, while the same adult pre-recorded does not. So for the under-three set the useful frame is not screen-versus-no-screen, it is responsive-versus-broadcast. A video call with a person answering back teaches. A polished cartoon covering the same word largely does not, yet.

cards.hook: Models read the start and end of your prompt. The middle blurs.
cards.body: Give a model a long context and ask it to use a fact buried inside, and accuracy depends heavily on where that fact sits. Performance is highest when the needed information is at the very beginning or the very end, and it sags in the middle. Researchers named the effect **'lost in the middle.'** The attention pattern is roughly U-shaped, not uniform, so a critical instruction dropped into the center of a long context can be quietly underweighted even though it is technically present and retrievable. The build implication: put the task and the load-bearing constraints at the top or the bottom, never in the soft middle.
cards.depth: Two practical moves. First, restate the actual task at the end of a long prompt, after the reference material, so it lands in the high-attention zone. Second, do not pad: adding marginally relevant context can shove the important part into the weak middle and lower accuracy, so retrieval that returns fewer, better chunks often beats returning more. Position is a lever you control for free.

cards.hook: Implied vol beats realized most months. That spread is the wage.
cards.body: Over long samples of index options, option-implied volatility sits a few points above the volatility that later shows up in the underlying. Sellers of that insurance collect the difference, the **variance risk premium**, and it is one of the most persistent edges in markets. But it is not a mispricing to arbitrage away. It is payment for holding a position that loses badly in crashes, exactly when your other assets fall too. The premium is the fee for absorbing that correlated tail. It pays steadily, then hands some back all at once.
cards.depth: The premium concentrates in downside strikes, which is why put skew is steep and why naive 'sell the wings' books look brilliant right up until a Volmageddon. The honest read: this is risk transfer, not alpha. Size it like insurance underwriting, where one bad year can erase several good ones, and the edge only compounds if you survive the payout.

cards.hook: Praise seems to hurt performance, criticism seems to help. Both illusions.
cards.body: Israeli flight instructors told Kahneman that praising a cadet after a great maneuver was followed by a worse one, while chewing out a bad maneuver was followed by improvement. So praise hurt and punishment worked. Both conclusions were **regression to the mean** wearing a causal mask. Exceptional results are part skill, part luck, and the luck does not repeat, so the next attempt drifts back toward average no matter what you said. Intervene right after any extreme outcome and the expected bounce-back will flatter or frame whatever you did.
cards.depth: This quietly corrupts trading journals and management alike. Cut a strategy after its worst month and it 'recovers' once you are out. Reward a trader after a hot streak and they cool. The fix is a control: compare against the base rate of what follows extremes anyway, not against your memory of what you changed. Mean reversion is the null hypothesis your intervention has to beat.

cards.hook: A second person in the room does your regulating for you.
cards.body: Body doubling means working next to someone, in person or on a video call, while you each do your own separate task. It works because ADHD is a deficit of **self-directed regulation**, not of ability, and another person's presence supplies from outside the structure your prefrontal system supplies unreliably from inside. Their attention raises the task's salience and adds a thin thread of accountability, so starting and staying both cost less. Nothing is delegated and no one touches your work. You are borrowing an external regulator to run an internal function.
cards.depth: This is why the same task is impossible alone and easy in a cafe or on a coworking call. Choose a partner you would rather not look idle in front of, and keep the task visible between you. The mechanism is identical to the one behind deadlines and public commitments: outsource the executive function you cannot summon on command.

cards.hook: Your fully AI-generated ad may belong to no one, including you.
cards.body: US copyright protects works of human authorship, and courts have held that output generated autonomously by a machine has no author to protect. The D.C. Circuit and the Copyright Office have both landed there: an image a model produces from your prompt is, standing alone, **uncopyrightable**. Prompts are treated as instructions, not authorship, because you do not control the output the way an author controls a sentence. The trap is assuming that elaborate prompting earns you a copyright. It does not. What you can protect is the human selection, arrangement, and editing you layer on top.
cards.depth: This inverts the usual worry. The risk is not only that a model copied someone else. It is that your own generated asset falls straight into the public domain, where a competitor can lawfully lift it. Register what a human meaningfully authored, document that contribution, and treat raw model output as unowned until a person shapes it into something.

cards.hook: Two words turn adjacent scenes into a story. Which two?
cards.body: You already met this one, from Trey Parker and Matt Stone. Read your outline and listen to the word joining each beat to the next. One connector is fatal; two are alive. Take a second before the reveal. The fatal link is 'and then,' which only sets events side by side. The living ones are **'but' and 'therefore.'** Reversal and consequence, the two shapes of causation that make an audience lean forward. If the only honest word between two scenes is 'and then,' they are adjacent, not connected, and the engine is off.
cards.depth: It bites hardest in the audio fiction you produce, where a listener has no picture to coast on and drifts the instant causation drops. Run the connective test on every episode outline before you record, and where a stretch only earns 'and then,' collapse it or find the 'but' that turns it. Recalling the rule cold, not just recognizing it, is what makes it fire while you are actually drafting.

cards.hook: Pinned at your strike, assignment is a coin flip.
cards.body: An option that expires a penny in the money is almost always exercised. One that finishes exactly at the strike is not. Holders decide based on their own book, after-hours moves, and rounding, so some exercise and some don't. That leaves you, the short, guessing. You close Friday believing you're flat, then learn over the weekend you were assigned, now unexpectedly long or short stock into Monday's gap. **The danger isn't the option, it's the position you didn't know you inherited.** Close or roll tight at-the-money shorts before the bell rather than betting on the coin flip.
cards.depth: The OCC auto-exercises anything at least a penny in the money, but the holder can file a contrary instruction until the deadline, and true at-the-money sits right on that knife edge. Cash-settled index options avoid share assignment entirely, which is one reason many premium sellers prefer them for expiration-week positions.

cards.hook: A judge handed AI plaintiffs the winning theory they ignored.
cards.body: In June 2025, a federal judge ruled Meta's training of its Llama models on copyrighted books was fair use, and the authors lost. But he said they lost because they argued the wrong case, not because Meta was right. The theory he flagged as the live one is **market dilution**: not that the model copied your book, but that it can now flood the market with competing works and gut demand for the originals. Most practitioners are still fighting over the input, whether their text sat in the training set. The judge signaled the next war is on the output.
cards.depth: The same week, a different San Francisco judge reached the opposite emphasis in the Anthropic case, calling the training 'exceedingly transformative.' Two judges, two roadmaps: one for defendants on transformation, one for plaintiffs on market harm. Fair use is a four-factor balance, and 2025 showed the fourth factor, effect on the market, is where these cases will actually be decided.

cards.hook: The fills your backtest assumes are the ones you'd miss.
cards.body: A backtest fills your order at the closing or mid price. Live, a resting limit order only executes when someone crosses it, which happens precisely when the market is moving through your price against you. So the trades you actually get filled on are adversely selected: you buy right before it keeps falling, you sell right before it keeps rising. **Mean-reversion strategies are flattered worst**, because the clean reversion trades are exactly the ones where nobody would have hit your resting order. The backtest booked profits on fills that, in the real book, never would have happened.
cards.depth: One partial check: re-run assuming you cross to the far touch and pay the spread, and add a fill probability below one for passive orders. If the edge evaporates, it was living inside the fill assumption, not the signal. Marketable orders dodge the selection bias but pay the spread every time, which is its own drag. Either way, the mid-price fill is a fiction.

cards.hook: ADHD's core deficit isn't attention. It's the missing pause.
cards.body: Barkley's model reframes the whole disorder: the primary deficit is response inhibition, the split-second pause between a stimulus and your reaction to it. Attention, working memory, and emotional control all sit downstream of that pause, because the pause is what buys the time to deploy them. Miss it, and you've acted before the executive machinery could load. The practical consequence: **you can't reliably manufacture the pause from the inside, so build it on the outside.** Put physical friction between you and the distractor. Log out, move the phone to another room. You're not adding willpower. You're rebuilding the gap the brain skips.
cards.depth: This is also why 'just focus' fails as advice: focus is a downstream product, not the lever. The lever is the environment around the pause. It reframes distraction too. The distractor isn't beating your attention, it's beating your inhibition, arriving before you could decline it. Change what can reach you in that first unguarded instant.

cards.hook: In 2018, short-vol funds hedged themselves off a cliff.
cards.body: February 5, 2018. Volatility had been dead for a year, and a crowd of inverse-VIX products, the largest called XIV, paid you to bet it stayed dead. Each had to rebalance daily by buying VIX futures whenever volatility rose. That afternoon it rose, so they bought, which pushed the futures higher, which forced them to buy more. The loop ran until XIV lost roughly 96% in hours and was shut down. **When a crowded trade's required hedging feeds the very thing it's exposed to, it becomes its own accelerant.** The move didn't kill them. Their reaction to it did.
cards.depth: The rebalance buying was concentrated in the last hour, which is why the worst of it landed near the close. The lesson rhymes with LTCM and the 2010 flash crash: leverage plus mechanical, price-triggered flows turns a normal move into a discontinuous one. Liquidity is thinnest exactly when everyone's rules demand the same trade at the same second.

cards.hook: A dividend is the only reason to exercise a call early.
cards.body: Textbooks say never exercise an American call early, because you throw away the remaining time value. The exception is the day before a stock goes ex-dividend. Holding the call, you do not collect the dividend; exercising converts it to stock in time to capture the payout. It is only worth it when the dividend exceeds the call's remaining extrinsic value, which happens on deep in-the-money calls with little time value left. **Miss that window and your short call gets assigned when you least expect it.** The assignment is not random. It is a rational dividend grab.
cards.depth: This is why brokers flag early-assignment risk around ex-dividend dates on short in-the-money calls. If you are short a call carrying less extrinsic value than the upcoming dividend, assume you will be assigned. The defensive move is to close or roll before the ex-dividend date, not gamble on the counterparty's inattention.

cards.hook: The 2023 guild deal splits digital replicas into two kinds.
cards.body: The 2023 SAG-AFTRA contract does not treat all AI likenesses the same. An **employment-based digital replica** is built from work the performer actually did on that production; an independently created digital replica is one the studio makes from other sources or from scratch. The distinction drives the money. For the employment-based kind, the performer must consent and generally be paid for the days the replica is used, as if they had worked them. Practitioners who lump both together miss that consent and compensation hinge on how the replica was created, not just on whether it resembles the actor.
cards.depth: The taxonomy matters for drafting. A blanket 'digital replica' consent clause can be under-inclusive or overreaching, because the guild floor attaches different rights to each category, plus a separate bucket for fully synthetic performers with no underlying human. Get it wrong and you either shortchange a payment or claim a consent the performer never actually gave.

cards.hook: Adding a detail can only lower a probability, never raise it.

cards.body: Kahneman and Tversky described Linda: a philosophy major, outspoken on social justice. Asked which is more likely, that she is a bank teller, or a bank teller and a feminist, most people pick the second. It cannot be. Feminist bank tellers sit inside the set of bank tellers, so that group is **always at least as improbable as the larger category alone**. Detail makes a story feel representative, and representativeness gets mistaken for probability. The more vivid and specific a scenario, the more plausible it feels and the less likely it actually is.
cards.depth: The trap shows up wherever you build a case. A detailed trial narrative, a market thesis with five confirming reasons, a granular forecast: each added clause feels like evidence but multiplies the ways the whole can be wrong. Strip a prediction to its load-bearing claim and score that, not the story wrapped around it.

cards.hook: How many items does working memory really hold? Not seven.
cards.body: You saw that Miller's famous 'seven plus or minus two' is mostly a myth for raw capacity. Take a beat before the number lands. Once researchers like Nelson Cowan stripped out the rehearsal and chunking that inflate the count, the honest limit came in near **four chunks**. So the checklist you are about to hand someone, the interface you are designing, the spoken instruction to your kid: if it asks them to juggle more than about four fresh things at once, it exceeds the hardware. Chunk it, or put the overflow on paper.
cards.depth: Retrieval is the point of this card, not the fact. Every time you pull 'four, not seven' back out of memory instead of rereading it, you deepen the trace. The applied version is a rule you will use this week: assume four, and anything past four needs external scaffolding, whether a written list, a template, or a visible countdown.

cards.hook: The marshmallow test mostly measured the household, not willpower.
cards.body: The 1970s Stanford studies claimed a preschooler who waited for a second treat did better in life decades later. A 2018 replication with a far larger, more representative sample told a quieter story. Once researchers controlled for family income and home environment, **much of the predictive power faded**. Waiting was largely a proxy for a stable, resourced household, where a child has good reason to trust that a promised reward will actually arrive. The lesson is not to drill your toddler on delay. It is that trust and stability teach patience better than a stopwatch.
cards.depth: There is a deeper mechanism worth keeping. Delay of gratification is not a fixed trait a child either has or lacks; it is partly a rational read of the environment. Kids who have learned that promises get broken grab the sure thing, correctly. Change the reliability of the world around them and their patience changes with it.

cards.hook: An at-the-money call's delta is above 0.50, not at it.
cards.body: Struck at the forward, a call's d1 term equals half sigma-root-T, which is positive. So its delta, N(d1), sits just above 0.50, and it climbs with more time or higher vol. The reason is structural: a lognormal price has its median below its mean, so the strike that gives a true coin-flip finish lies slightly out of the money relative to the forward. **A 'symmetric' at-the-money straddle is quietly long delta.** Retail treats 50-delta as the ATM anchor, but the forward, not spot, is the real center of mass.
cards.depth: How much? At 20% vol and one month, half-sigma-root-T is about 0.03, nudging delta to roughly 0.51. Stretch to a year and it is near 0.54. Small, yes. But your 'delta-neutral' short straddle then needs a few shares of hedge you probably never put on.

cards.hook: The Warhol ruling quietly reloaded every AI fair-use defense.
cards.body: In 2023 the Supreme Court, in Warhol v Goldsmith, narrowed transformative use: a new meaning or message no longer saves a copy if the use serves the **same commercial purpose** as the original. AI training defenses had leaned hard on transformativeness. Now a plaintiff can argue that a model trained on their work to make competing work shares that work's purpose, weakening factor one before factor four is even reached. Practitioners still cite pre-Warhol wins like Google v Oracle as if the ground has not shifted. It has.
cards.depth: The nuance the headlines missed: Warhol touched only factor one, and the Court called it a narrow holding. But 'same purpose' is exactly the wedge in AI suits, since a model that outputs marketable images arguably competes with the images it trained on. Whether courts stretch it from one Prince photo to a billion-image corpus is the open question.

cards.hook: Your reminder system stops working the day it stops being new.
cards.body: The mechanism is salience. An ADHD brain allocates attention by how much a cue stands out, not by how much it matters. A new checklist, a fresh sticky note, a just-built app all grab you because novelty spikes the signal. Two weeks later the cue is furniture and your eye slides past it. This is **tool decay**, and it is why every system you build works for a while and then quietly dies. The fix is not a better system. It is changing the cue's form on a schedule: move it, recolor it, reword it, so novelty keeps the signal alive.
cards.depth: Practical version: stop chasing the perfect permanent system, because it will decay no matter how good it is. Build one that is cheap to refresh instead. A whiteboard you rewrite every Sunday beats an elegant app you stop seeing by Wednesday. The refresh is the feature, not a sign the tool failed.

cards.hook: Fifteen years of daily data is not 3,750 independent tests.

cards.body: A backtest brags about sample size in observations, but statistics only reward **independent** observations. Daily returns clump into regimes: a low-vol bull, a crash, a recovery. A strategy fit on 2010 to 2021 mostly saw one macro environment, falling rates and rising multiples, dressed up as thousands of data points. Its real out-of-sample count might be two or three. That is why models 'validated on 15 years' die in year sixteen. They were tuned against a handful of regimes while reading the calendar as if it were the sample.
cards.depth: The discipline: count regimes, not rows. Ask how many genuinely different environments the data spans, rate cycles, vol regimes, liquidity states, and treat that as your degrees of freedom. A Sharpe earned across four regimes outranks one earned across four thousand correlated days inside a single regime.

cards.hook: You met the seven-year rule. What made it bite?
cards.body: The cap comes from **California Labor Code section 2855**, which holds any personal-service contract to seven years. Studios used to gut it by tolling the clock every time an actor refused a role and drew a suspension, stretching a seven-year deal across a decade. In 1944 Olivia de Havilland won the reading that seven years means seven calendar years of the contract's life, not seven years of service actually rendered. That is the whole mechanism: suspensions stopped pausing the clock. It is why the statute still governs long artist and recording deals today.
cards.depth: Modern echo: recording artists have invoked 2855 to break out of multi-album deals, running the same calendar-years logic. Labels push back with claims for undelivered albums. The tension De Havilland pried open, service rendered versus term elapsed, has never fully closed.

cards.hook: Selling index options is mostly selling correlation.
cards.body: An index option's vol is built from two ingredients: component vols and the correlation binding them. Back out the correlation implied by index options versus single-name options and you find it **persistently trades above what correlation subsequently realizes**. That gap is why the index variance risk premium runs fatter than the average single-stock premium - the difference is a correlation risk premium. Dispersion desks harvest it directly: short index vol, long a basket of single-name vols, sized so aggregate vol exposure roughly cancels. What remains is a pure bet that stocks move together less than the market fears. Sell an index straddle and that is mostly what you are collecting.
cards.depth: The premium exists because correlation spikes exactly when it hurts. In a crash, pairwise correlations lurch toward one, index vol explodes relative to the basket, and short-correlation books take their worst mark. Like the vol risk premium itself, it is insurance income: paid for bearing a left tail that arrives on everyone's worst day. CBOE's implied correlation indexes let you watch the spread directly.

cards.hook: In London, Stable Diffusion's weights are not a copy.
cards.body: In November 2025 the UK High Court delivered the first major ruling on whether an AI model is itself an infringing copy of its training data. Getty had dropped its core training and output claims mid-trial, leaving secondary infringement: did Stability import an 'infringing copy' of Getty's images into the UK in the form of Stable Diffusion? No, held the court, because the weights **store and reproduce none of the training images**. The model is not a copy, even though copies were unquestionably used to make it. Getty salvaged a narrow trademark win over generated watermarks. The model-as-derivative-of-its-corpus theory just took its first direct hit on the merits.
cards.depth: The ruling blesses less than headlines suggest. Getty abandoned the training and output claims for jurisdictional and evidentiary reasons, so UK law on training itself remains open, and Getty's parallel US case against Stability continues in Delaware. But the weights holding travels: if a model is not a copy of its corpus, distributing the model is not distributing the works.

cards.hook: Two underwriters, same file, quotes 55 percent apart.
cards.body: When Kahneman's team asked an insurer's executives how far apart two underwriters would land pricing the same policy, the guesses centered near 10 percent. The audit's reported answer: a median gap of 55 percent. The mechanism is that **noise is invisible in the single case**. A biased shop at least leaves a pattern you can catch; noisy judgments each look reasonable alone, and the scatter only appears when two professionals judge the identical file, which almost no organization stages. In squared-error terms, noise degrades accuracy exactly as much as the same amount of bias. Any desk pricing deals or grading risk runs a lottery it has never audited.
cards.depth: System noise splits into level noise (some graders run harsh), pattern noise (idiosyncratic reactions to specific cases), and occasion noise (the same person on a different day). The cheap countermeasure is decision hygiene: collect independent judgments before anyone talks, then aggregate. Averaging independent reads cuts noise by the square root of the count - two readers buy roughly a 29 percent reduction.

cards.hook: Six hours a night, and you stop noticing the damage.
cards.body: In the classic Penn dose-response study, adults limited to six hours of sleep for two weeks accumulated attention lapses equivalent to going one to two full nights without sleep. The unnerving part was the self-ratings. Subjective sleepiness rose for a few days, then flattened, while objective performance kept sliding all fourteen days: **the felt sense of impairment decouples from the impairment itself**. Chronic short sleepers recalibrate 'normal' around the deficit and report feeling roughly fine while performing like the acutely deprived. So 'do I feel rested?' is nearly worthless as a gauge. Only the objective signal stays honest - reaction-time data, the tracker's trend, actual hours in bed.
cards.depth: The eight-hour control group held steady across the two weeks, and the four-hour group degraded materially faster, reaching total-deprivation territory within the same window. Nothing in the data suggested adaptation; the curves never flattened. For a CPAP-plus-tracker setup, treat duration trends as the leading indicator and treat 'I feel fine' as lagging, self-serving data.

cards.hook: If knowing isn't the bottleneck, where does the fix go?
cards.body: A few days ago a card carried Barkley's sharpest clinical claim: in ADHD, knowing what to do does not transfer to the moment of doing it. The bottleneck is performance, not information. So, before reading on: where did he say the intervention has to live? Take the beat. His answer was the **point of performance** - the exact place and second the behavior is needed. The pill bottle sits on the coffee machine, the signed check is clipped to the exit door. When one of your fixes keeps failing, check its address first; it is almost always installed upstream of the moment instead of inside it.
cards.depth: Recalling this beats rereading it; retrieval is the rehearsal that actually strengthens the trace. To make it operational: pick the one commitment that slipped this week, name the exact moment it should have fired, and physically move its cue there. If the fix cannot be placed at that address, it is a wish, not a system.

cards.hook: A variance swap is a whole strip of options, not one.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><line x1="55" y1="30" x2="55" y2="200" stroke="#35302a" stroke-width="1.5"/><line x1="55" y1="200" x2="370" y2="200" stroke="#35302a" stroke-width="1.5"/><path d="M65 48 C 130 150, 200 182, 365 193" fill="none" stroke="#d9a441" stroke-width="2.5"/><text x="60" y="24" fill="#a89f8d" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="14">weight per strike</text><text x="250" y="222" fill="#a89f8d" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="14">strike K →</text><text x="92" y="72" fill="#7fb4a2" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="15">∝ 1/K²</text><text x="150" y="118" fill="#a89f8d" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="13">low strikes carry the most weight</text></svg>
cards.body: A variance swap pays the gap between realized and strike variance, and its fair strike cannot come from any single at-the-money option. To hedge it, a dealer holds a **strip of options weighted by one over strike squared**, so far-out-of-the-money puts carry the most weight. That is why the fair strike sits above at-the-money implied vol: the skew priced into cheap downside puts gets loaded heavily. The VIX is built exactly this way, which is why it is a variance measure and not an option price.
cards.depth: The 1/K-squared weighting drops straight out of the replication of a log contract: to match that payoff, each strike's weight is inversely proportional to its square. Practically, your downside wings, not the body, set the number. Misjudge deep-put pricing and your whole variance mark is wrong.

cards.hook: A convincing soundalike can infringe even if it isn't your voice.
cards.body: Right of publicity reaches imitation, not just recording. In Midler v. Ford, a studio hired an impersonator after Bette Midler declined, and the Ninth Circuit held that deliberately evoking a distinctive voice to sell a product is actionable. Tom Waits later won the same argument, with damages. The 2024 rhyme was OpenAI's 'Sky' voice, which drew Scarlett Johansson's objection and was pulled, though the company said it hired a different actor. For AI voice work the rule is old: **sounding like someone can be enough**, whoever's cords made the sound.
cards.depth: Midler and Waits are Ninth Circuit, so they bind in California, where most of this work lands. The doctrine turns on a voice being distinctive and the imitation being intentional. A generic voice is not protected; a signature one is, and a model trained to evoke it inherits that exposure.

cards.hook: Every 'quick email check' is a costly reload, not a break.
cards.body: Switching tasks forces your brain to dump the current mental state and rebuild the next one. For an ADHD brain the penalty lands harder, because reloading the dropped context leans on **working memory, the exact system that runs short**. So a thirty-second glance at email is not a rest; it is a demolition of the state you spent minutes assembling. The move is structural: batch like tasks, and treat 'I'll just quickly check' as an expensive switch to refuse, not a harmless pause. Guard one block, finish one thing.
cards.depth: The cost is not the seconds spent away; it is the minutes to rebuild afterward. Put a physical barrier on the cheap switches: close the tab, phone in another room, notifications off for the block. You are not fighting laziness, you are lowering the number of reloads per hour.

cards.hook: One actress's lawsuit capped every Hollywood contract at seven years.
cards.body: Studios once held stars on seven-year deals, then added the length of every suspension: refuse a role and the clock paused, so seven years could stretch past a decade. Olivia de Havilland sued Warner Bros. and, in 1944, California's courts read Labor Code section 2855 literally. Seven calendar years means seven calendar years, not seven years of actual work. Overnight the studios lost their power to hold talent indefinitely. The 'De Havilland Law' still caps personal service contracts today, which is why **a single suit reset the balance of power** for eighty years.
cards.depth: Section 2855 is still litigated; recording artists have invoked it against long album commitments. The mechanism is durable because it is a bright-line statute, not a balancing test. Bright lines are hard to erode, which is exactly why studios could not suspend their way around it once the court fixed the meaning of a year.

cards.hook: If your beats connect with 'and then,' the story is dead.
cards.body: Trey Parker and Matt Stone teach one editing test: read your outline and see whether each beat links to the next with 'and then' or with **'but' or 'therefore.'** 'And then' is a list, one thing after another, no momentum. 'But' introduces a reversal; 'therefore' introduces a consequence. Both create causation, and causation is what makes an audience lean forward instead of drift. Run the test on any sequence of scenes: if you can only say 'and then,' the beats are merely adjacent, not connected, and the engine is off.
cards.depth: The rule scales down to the paragraph and up to the act. It also diagnoses the fix, not just the flaw: a dead 'and then' usually means a missing decision or reaction that would have turned it into a 'therefore.' Add the causal link and the same events start to move.

cards.hook: Half Kelly keeps three-quarters of the growth, a quarter of the variance.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><line x1="40" y1="200" x2="372" y2="200" stroke="#35302a" stroke-width="1"/><line x1="40" y1="36" x2="40" y2="200" stroke="#35302a" stroke-width="1"/><polyline points="40,200 80,130 120,80 160,50 200,40 240,50 280,80 320,130 360,200" fill="none" stroke="#d9a441" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="120" y1="80" x2="120" y2="200" stroke="#7fb4a2" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="4 3"/><line x1="200" y1="40" x2="200" y2="200" stroke="#35302a" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="4 3"/><circle cx="120" cy="80" r="4" fill="#7fb4a2"/><circle cx="200" cy="40" r="4" fill="#d9a441"/><text x="200" y="30" fill="#a89f8d" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle">full Kelly</text><text x="126" y="74" fill="#a89f8d" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="13">half Kelly = 3/4 growth</text><text x="120" y="216" fill="#a89f8d" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle">0.5x</text><text x="200" y="216" fill="#a89f8d" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle">1x</text><text x="360" y="216" fill="#a89f8d" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle">2x</text><text x="22" y="118" fill="#a89f8d" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="13" transform="rotate(-90 22 118)" text-anchor="middle">growth rate</text></svg>
cards.body: The growth-rate curve as a function of bet fraction is a dome, peaking at full Kelly and falling back to zero at twice Kelly. Because it is flat near the top and the penalty is quadratic, betting half of Kelly still captures **three-quarters of the maximum growth rate**, while variance, which scales with fraction squared, drops to a quarter. Overbetting is punished asymmetrically: past the peak you add risk and lose growth at the same time. Kelly assumes you know your edge exactly, and you never do, so fractional Kelly is the honest default.
cards.depth: The dome is g(f) roughly proportional to f times edge minus f squared times variance over two. Maximize it and you get the Kelly fraction; plug in half of it and the algebra returns exactly three-quarters. Near the optimum, undershooting is cheap and overshooting is not.

cards.hook: Stop while the next step is still obvious.
cards.body: In ADHD the expensive moment is not the work, it is the restart. Re-entering a paused task means paying the same activation threshold that made starting hard the first time, and a cold task offers no foothold. So do not run each session until you are empty and stuck. Stop at a point where the next move is trivial and already known: a half-finished sentence, the test written but not yet run. You are buying down tomorrow's **activation energy** by leaving a foothold today. Hemingway did this on purpose, ending while it was still going well so beginning again was easy.
cards.depth: The mechanism is task initiation, the self-directed action ADHD taxes most heavily. A warm task with an obvious next step barely requires initiation. A cold one requires all of it. Move the friction to the moment you have the most momentum, not the moment you have the least.

cards.hook: Consent to build the replica is not consent to use it.
cards.body: SAG-AFTRA's 2023 film and television contract, ratified after the strike, treats a digital replica as two separate gates, not one. A performer must give informed consent to create the replica, accompanied by a reasonably specific description of how it will be used, and that description is the leash. Deploying the replica in new material beyond that description requires **separate consent and separate compensation**. A blanket grant, the perpetual any-and-all-uses language boilerplate loves, does not clear the bar. The practitioner error is treating consent-to-create as a license to reuse. It is not.
cards.depth: This rhymes with California's AB 2602: specificity is doing the enforcement work in both regimes. A clause that cannot say what the replica is for is a clause a court or a union can unwind. Vague scope, once the cheap default, is now the exposure.

cards.hook: The short leg that makes the backtest is unborrowable.
cards.body: Long-short backtests usually assume you can short any name at zero cost. In reality the shorts that generate the alpha, heavily shorted small caps, distressed names, crowded meme stocks, are exactly the ones that are **hard or impossible to borrow**. Borrow fees on those can run double digits annualized, and sometimes there are no shares to locate at any price. The paper edge concentrates in the leg you cannot actually harvest. Strip the unborrowable names and rerun, and a strategy that looked like free money often flattens into the cost of the borrow.
cards.depth: This is selection bias hiding inside the cost model. The market charges the most to short exactly what everyone wants to short, and that fee is the market pricing away your anomaly. A backtest that fills shorts for free is quietly assuming the crowd left money on the table.

cards.hook: Clone an expert's own past calls. Why does the copy win?
cards.body: You built a plain linear model from an expert's own decisions, the same cues, the weights her calls imply, then let it replace her going forward. It reliably beats her. Take a beat before the reason. It is not that the model knows more. It knows strictly less. What it drops is **noise**: her inconsistency across identical cases, the mood and fatigue and last-case echo riding on top of an otherwise valid rule. She supplies the weights, then corrupts them with random variation. Strip the variation, keep the signal. Goldberg showed this in the 1960s; Kahneman later made noise the whole subject.
cards.depth: Why it matters again: your own trade checklist and your own redline standards are the expert. Written once and followed mechanically, they beat the discretionary you who overrides them on a Tuesday. Most overrides are not insight. They are noise wearing the costume of judgment.

cards.hook: At implied vol, your theta exactly pays for your gamma.
cards.body: Sell a delta-hedged option and two forces fight. Theta pays you daily for time decay. Gamma bleeds you every time the underlying moves, because re-hedging locks in losses at the highs and lows. Priced at the option's implied vol, those two are engineered to cancel in expectation: the market sets theta to exactly compensate the gamma you will pay if the stock realizes its implied vol. So a hedged short option carries **zero expected edge at implied vol**. Your entire profit is the gap between implied and what actually gets realized. You are not short options. You are short realized variance.
cards.depth: This is why selling 'expensive' options is not automatically edge. Expensive means high implied vol; if realized comes in just as high, theta and gamma wash and you netted transaction costs against yourself. The variance risk premium, implied minus realized running a few vol points on average, is the only durable reason the short side pays.

cards.hook: Turn time into a shrinking wedge you can see.
cards.body: ADHD blunts the internal sense of time passing, what Barkley calls **time blindness**: the future does not feel like it is approaching, so urgency stays flat until a deadline is nearly on top of you. A digital clock does not fix this. It shows a number, not a rate. An analog countdown timer that drains a colored wedge converts the invisible interval into a physical quantity that visibly disappears. You are not motivating yourself harder. You are giving a time-blind brain an external sense organ for duration.
cards.depth: The move generalizes: any deadline you cannot feel, make continuous and visible. A progress bar, a burning candle, a timer sitting on the desk. The point is not the countdown itself but converting a discounted future event into present sensory input, which is the one channel a time-blind system reliably registers.

cards.hook: Tennessee protects your voice, and targets the cloning tool itself.
cards.body: Most right-of-publicity statutes grew up around image and name. Tennessee's ELVIS Act, effective July 1, 2024, was the first US law to add **voice as its own protected right** and, more importantly, to reach upstream. It creates liability not just for whoever publishes an unauthorized vocal clone but for distributing any tool or service whose primary function is producing one. That is the frontier move practitioners keep missing: the exposure attaches to the model and platform makers, not only the end user who hit generate.
cards.depth: Compare California's AB 1836 and AB 2602, which regulate the use of a digital replica of a performer; Tennessee instead went after the supply chain. For anyone building or licensing voice AI, the diligence question is no longer only 'did we get consent for this voice' but 'could our product be characterized as a tool whose main purpose is unauthorized replication.'

cards.hook: Positive expected value can still ruin almost every player.
cards.body: Offer a bet that adds 50% to your stake on heads and cuts it 40% on tails, fifty-fifty. The arithmetic mean is +5% per flip, so a room full of gamblers, taken together, gets richer. But you are not the room. You are one person compounding one sequence, and the **time-average growth rate is negative**: heads then tails multiplies your money by 1.5 times 0.6, which is 0.9. Repeat and almost every individual path decays toward zero. The mean describes parallel worlds. You live one. This gap is non-ergodicity, and it is why bet sizing, not edge, decides survival.
cards.depth: The ensemble average and the time average agree for additive processes and diverge for multiplicative ones, which is nearly everything involving wealth. Kelly sizing is the operational fix: it maximizes the time-average growth rate, not the expected value, which is exactly why a positive-EV bet can still be too big to survive.

cards.hook: Working memory holds about four items, not the famous seven.
cards.body: Miller's 1956 'magical number seven plus or minus two' became the most-cited number in psychology and is mostly wrong for raw capacity. When later researchers, notably Nelson Cowan, blocked the tricks people use to inflate the count, rehearsal and chunking, the real limit of pure working memory landed closer to **four chunks**. The practical consequence is not trivia. Any instruction, checklist, or interface that expects someone to juggle more than about four novel elements at once is exceeding the hardware. Design past four by chunking, or by putting the rest on paper.
cards.depth: Chunking is how experts fake a bigger buffer: a grandmaster sees one meaningful pattern where a novice sees six pieces, spending one slot instead of six. The capacity did not grow, the units did. This is also why externalizing, writing the other items down, is not a crutch but the correct response to a fixed limit.

cards.hook: A calendar spread bets on the term structure, not direction.
cards.body: Sell a near-dated option, buy a far-dated one at the same strike, and retail calls it a theta trade. Go deeper: you are long forward volatility. The position's value is set by the difference between near-term realized vol and the vol implied for the back month, and by how the whole term structure shifts and rolls. **A calendar can lose money even with spot pinned at the strike** if the back-month implied vol collapses. You are not renting time decay. You are taking a view on the shape of the vol curve.
cards.depth: This is why calendars behave best when back-month implied vol is stable or rising and near-term realized stays quiet. A vol-crush after an earnings event can gut a calendar you opened to harvest that same event. The greek that matters is not theta. It is vega spread across two expirations, plus the term-structure roll.

cards.hook: Your ADHD med was engineered to have no kick.
cards.body: Lisdexamfetamine is a prodrug: the molecule you swallow is inert. It only becomes active dextroamphetamine after enzymes in your bloodstream slowly cleave off an attached amino acid. That rate-limiting step is the whole point. It smooths the onset, stretches the duration, and blunts the euphoric spike that drives abuse. The practical move follows from the mechanism: **do not judge the dose by a felt surge.** It was designed not to produce one. Titrate on how your afternoon and evening actually function, not on whether you noticed it kick in an hour after breakfast.
cards.depth: The amino acid is L-lysine, and the cleavage happens largely in red blood cells, which is why food and stomach pH barely move its absorption. Compare Strattera, a pure norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor with a different mechanism entirely. Same diagnosis, different pharmacology, and the wrong mental model of 'kick' makes you over-titrate chasing a feeling the drug is built to suppress.

cards.hook: A forecast is only as honest as its scoring rule.
cards.body: Say you are '70% confident' all year. Were you right? You cannot know without a scoring rule that punishes both timid and reckless probabilities. Proper scoring rules, like the Brier or logarithmic score, are built so your best strategy is to report your true belief; shading toward 0 or 100 to game them costs you on average. The score decomposes into two parts, **calibration and resolution.** Calibration asks whether your 70%s happen 70% of the time; resolution asks whether you bother to say 95% when you should. A single accuracy number hides which one you lack.
cards.depth: The distinction is why two forecasters with identical hit rates are not equal. A weather service that always says '30% rain' in a 30%-rain climate is perfectly calibrated and perfectly useless. Resolution is the skill of moving off the base rate when you actually know something. Keep a ledger and you can see, over time, which half you are missing.

cards.hook: A film grossed nearly $300M and 'lost money' on paper.
cards.body: Coming to America earned roughly $288 million worldwide in 1988. On the studio's books it never showed a net profit. Art Buchwald, who had sold Paramount the story idea for a share of net profits, sued and won: in 1990 a California judge ruled the contract's net-profit definition **unconscionable.** The mechanism is arithmetic, not fraud. Gross participants take their cut off the top, then a distribution fee, then interest charged on the negative cost, then studio overhead figured as a percentage of costs that already include overhead. 'Net profit' is engineered to approach zero.
cards.depth: The lesson generalizes past Hollywood: whenever the other side controls the definition of the number you are paid on, the number is theirs to shape. Gross players, the stars and directors with leverage, get paid off a defined, hard-to-manipulate figure. Everyone paid on 'net' is paid on a formula. Structure your deal on gross, adjusted gross, or a fixed number, never on someone else's net.

cards.hook: Which ratio makes a time bomb look like a bond?
cards.body: Think back to the metric that rewards a smooth track record no matter how ugly the tail is. Give yourself a beat. It is the **Sharpe ratio.** It divides return by standard deviation, and standard deviation cannot see skew or kurtosis, the two moments where option-selling risk actually lives. So a strategy that drips small gains and rarely detonates posts a beautiful Sharpe right up until the month that erases years. Rank candidate strategies by Sharpe and you systematically promote the ones most able to ruin you.
cards.depth: You saw this a week ago and it still governs how you screen. The fix is not to abandon Sharpe but to pair it with a tail metric: Sortino, max drawdown, or the ratio of worst month to average month. Any screen that ranks on a single volatility-based number will keep handing you the short-premium strategies that look best precisely because their disaster has not printed yet.

cards.hook: Same strike, same implied vol for put and call.
cards.body: Retail traders eyeball an out-of-the-money put quoted richer than the equidistant call and conclude the put carries more implied volatility. It cannot. Put-call parity is a **model-free no-arbitrage identity**. Knowing the call's price at a strike fixes the put's price, given the forward. Back out implied vol from either and you get the same number, because the map from vol to price is monotonic. The skew you see is real, but it lives across strikes, not between the put and call at one strike. A gap there is a box-spread arbitrage, not an edge.
cards.depth: The forward matters. Dividends and carry shift the parity line, so a comparison that ignores them can manufacture a phantom vol gap. Screen a skew by strike and moneyness, never by call-versus-put, or you will chase differences that exist only in stale quotes from your data feed.

cards.hook: Training on the books was fair use. Pirating them was not.
cards.body: In Bartz v. Anthropic, decided June 2025, Judge Alsup called training a model on copyrighted books **exceedingly transformative** and squarely fair use. Then he split the question the industry keeps blurring. How you obtained the corpus is a different legal question from what you did with it. Downloading and warehousing pirated copies to build a permanent library was not excused by the eventual fair use, and that piracy headed toward trial. The parties later settled, reported at roughly $1.5 billion. The lesson for anyone assembling training data is that a clean use does not launder a dirty acquisition.
cards.depth: This pairs with Kadrey v. Meta. Kadrey said the use theory plaintiffs need is market dilution. Bartz says even a winning use theory does not cure unlawful sourcing. Provenance and transformation are now two separate gates, and a defendant has to clear both. Acquire the data lawfully, then argue fair use, not the reverse.

cards.hook: Bind the action to a cue, not to your intention.
cards.body: A goal held in mind, like 'call the client this afternoon,' leans on prospective memory and self-started action, the two things ADHD taxes hardest. An implementation intention rewires the job into **if situation X, then behavior Y**. For example, 'when I sit down after lunch, I open the client file first.' Gollwitzer's meta-analysis across dozens of studies found this if-then format produced a medium-to-large jump in follow-through. The mechanism is delegation. You pre-decide once, and the cue itself triggers the action, so starting no longer waits on you noticing the moment and choosing to begin.
cards.depth: The cue must be concrete and unavoidable, an event you will physically hit, not a clock time, because time blindness eats 'at 2pm.' Anchor it to something already in the flow: the first coffee, closing the laptop, the daycare drive. You are not adding willpower. You are moving the decision earlier, to a calmer moment when choosing is easy.

cards.hook: If no answer changes your move, do not run the test.
cards.body: Decision theory gives a clean rule for when to gather information. Its value is exactly zero if no possible result would change your choice. **The expected value of information is the payoff of your decision after learning, minus the payoff of your best decision now.** When those are equal, the data is entertainment, not input. Traders backtest one more variant that would not alter position size. Lawyers pull one more document that would not change the advice. The discipline is to name, in advance, which finding flips which action. If you cannot name one, the research is procrastination wearing a lab coat.
cards.depth: This is not a license to stay ignorant. A finding can change how strongly you act, not only whether you act, and that still counts. The trap is the study run for comfort, to feel diligent before doing what you were always going to do. Ask what would move, and by how much, first. A zero answer means zero value.

cards.hook: Chain twenty 95%-reliable steps. What's your finish rate?
cards.body: A few days back: an agent that nails each step 95% of the time, run twenty steps deep. Before you read on, estimate the odds the whole chain finishes clean. Most people guess somewhere in the eighties. The real number is **about 36%**, because 0.95 to the twentieth power does not care how good your prompt is. That is why the payoff was not sharper per-step instructions but recoverable failure: validators that catch bad output, checkpoints that retry one step instead of the whole run, and shorter dependent paths. It is yield math, the logic a factory runs on.
cards.depth: Why it matters again: under pressure the instinct is always to sharpen the prompt, the one lever that barely moves a long chain. Reliability compounds multiplicatively, so the wins live in architecture, not wording. Every time a run dies at step fifteen, ask whether step fifteen should have been catchable, not whether it should have been perfect.

cards.hook: Net-zero vega can still lose on a vol twist.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><line x1="50" y1="200" x2="370" y2="200" stroke="#35302a"/><line x1="50" y1="30" x2="50" y2="200" stroke="#35302a"/><polyline points="60,150 160,135 260,125 360,118" fill="none" stroke="#7fb4a2" stroke-width="2"/><polyline points="60,70 160,108 260,120 360,118" fill="none" stroke="#d9a441" stroke-width="2"/><text x="70" y="58" fill="#a89f8d" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="14">vol twist: front-end spike</text><text x="238" y="145" fill="#a89f8d" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="13">calm term structure</text><text x="55" y="216" fill="#a89f8d" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="13">short</text><text x="335" y="216" fill="#a89f8d" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="13">long</text><text x="30" y="40" fill="#a89f8d" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="13">IV</text></svg>
cards.body: Vega is not one number. It is a curve across expirations, and your book can sum to zero while being long front-month vol and short the back, or the reverse. When the **term structure twists** instead of shifting in parallel, that netted-out exposure comes alive. A short-dated spike with a calm back end hammers a position that read as vega-neutral on the risk screen. Bucket your vega by expiration, not into a single line, or the number is quietly lying to you.
cards.depth: This is why calendars and diagonals are term-structure trades, not directional ones. VIX futures usually sit in contango, and the front reacts hardest to shocks. A parallel-shift model of vol misprices every one of them. Any greek that assumes the whole surface moves together hides the risk that actually pays or bites.

cards.hook: California voids a digital-replica clause that is too vague.
cards.body: AB 2602, effective January 2025, added Labor Code section 927. It makes a contract provision permitting a **digital replica** of a performer unenforceable when two conditions both hold: the clause lacks a reasonably specific description of the intended uses, and the performer was not represented by a lawyer or a union bargaining for them. The blanket 'any and all uses, in perpetuity, throughout the universe' grant that boilerplate loves does not clear that bar. Specificity is now the price of enforceability, at least in California.
cards.depth: The statute targets the exact move studios reached for during the 2023 strikes: acquire broad replica rights cheap, in language the signer cannot parse. Read it alongside AB 1836, which requires estate consent for digital replicas of deceased performers. Two California statutes, one theme. The replica right no longer travels on vague paper.

cards.hook: Evidence moves you by its likelihood ratio, nothing else.
cards.body: Bayes says your posterior odds equal your prior odds times one quantity: the **likelihood ratio**, how much more probable the evidence is if the claim is true versus if it is false. A detail can be vivid, specific, and emotionally loaded and still carry a ratio near one, because it is equally likely under both stories. That evidence feels decisive and moves nothing. The right question is never 'does this fit my theory' but 'does this fit my theory better than the rival one.'
cards.depth: This is the engine under base-rate neglect. People swap the diagnostic question for a resemblance question: does the evidence look like the conclusion. Resemblance is not a likelihood ratio. A witness detail consistent with guilt but equally consistent with innocence is, formally, worthless, however it plays on the stand.

cards.hook: The fix has to sit where the behavior happens.
cards.body: Barkley's sharpest clinical claim: in ADHD, knowledge does not transfer to the moment of action. You can fully understand what to do and still not do it, because the bottleneck is **performance, not information**. So the intervention belongs at what he calls the point of performance, the exact place and time the behavior is needed. Not a reminder earlier that morning. The pill bottle on the coffee machine. The signed check clipped to the door. Move the cue to the moment, not upstream of it.
cards.depth: This is why insight-heavy approaches underperform here and environmental ones win. The deficit is executive, a gap between knowing and doing, so you engineer the physical world to close it. Externalize the rule into the spot where it fires. Willpower staged upstream is precisely the thing that keeps failing.

cards.hook: A range offer can out-anchor a single number.
cards.body: Conventional advice says never give a range, because you will get pinned to the bad end. The research complicates that. Ames and Mason found that a **bolstering-range offer**, where the low end is the number you actually want, often beats a precise point offer set at that same number. The range signals reasonableness and room while the counterpart anchors on the whole span, not just its floor. The failure mode is the opposite construction: a range whose top is your target. That one does get you pinned low.
cards.depth: Mechanism: the range widens the counterpart's read of your resistance point and adds a politeness signal that dampens aggressive countering, without conceding your anchor. Direction is everything. Anchor from strength, and let the span do the softening for you.

cards.hook: Delta is the risk-neutral odds, not your true odds.
cards.body: Retail lore says an option's delta approximates its probability of finishing in the money. It does approximate a probability, but the risk-neutral one, which already bakes in the market's price of risk. For an out-of-the-money put, the real-world chance of expiring worthless sits **above the delta-implied number**, because the pricing measure loads extra weight onto down moves that the physical world does not deliver. That gap is why systematically selling the 16-delta put pays: you collect against roughly 84% risk-neutral odds while the true odds of keeping the premium run higher.
cards.depth: Two forces open the gap. The risk-neutral drift is the risk-free rate rather than the higher real equity drift, and put skew prices downside volatility richer than stocks tend to realize it. Both push the risk-neutral probability of a down finish above the physical one. Measure that gap and you are measuring the variance risk premium directly.

cards.hook: ADHD does not weaken willpower. It steepens the discount curve.
cards.body: Delay discounting is how much a reward loses value as it moves into the future, and in ADHD the curve is steeper: a payoff two weeks out is worth far less right now than it is to a neurotypical brain. This is not a motivation deficit, it is a valuation defect. The move follows straight from the mechanism: **stop relying on distant consequences and manufacture a near one**. A body-double session today, a stake you forfeit tonight if the draft is not started, a reward that lands within the hour. You are not disciplining the curve, you are refusing to bet against it.
cards.depth: The pattern generalizes: steeper discounting predicts choosing the small-now over the large-later, and it does not respond to being told the large-later is smarter. It responds to changing the schedule. Medication flattens the curve somewhat; environment design does the rest. Design the payoff to arrive before the discount can eat it.
